notes.7: (a) A correct response was given by the majority of candidates. (b) (i) Most candidates gave responses indicating no change to the reading. (ii) A very large number of candidates incorrectly suggested that the pointer moved left or right. (iii) Similarly to Question (b)(ii) above, many candidates incorrectly suggested movement of the pointer but in the opposite direction to that stated in (b)(ii) . (iv) Many candidates recognised that the pointer would move but only the better candidates were able to gain full credit for appreciating that the pointer would deflect from side to side.
notes.9: (a) Very few candidates correctly identified the standard test of repelling the N pole of known magnet. Most described attracting an S pole or gave vague answers in terms of the use of iron filings or a compass. (b) Most candidates scored well on this question, the majority of candidates identifying the correct responses. (c) (i) Most candidates gave a correct response to this question. notes.12: This question was answered well by all but the weakest of candidates. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2014
notes.1a: Many candidates were aware of the need to divide distance by time, but few used the correct values. A common error was omitting to take account of the original plant height.
notes.1bi: The majority gained full credit for their responses, but a significant number lacked precision, plotting points in the wrong square or on the wrong day. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2014
notes.1bii: A large proportion of candidates recognised that the points were not on a straight line. Some candidates incorrectly drew on information from the table rather than the points on the graph.
notes.2a: This question was answered well by the better candidates. Common mistakes included the use of the term “extends” to explain extension, and responses that indicated the extension was the total length of the spring when a load had been added.
notes.2bii: This question was not well answered. The most common errors were in rearranging the equation W = mg and the lack of an appropriate unit. The information ‘Take the weight of 1 kg to be 10 N’ is given on the front of the Question Paper.
notes.3a: This question was well answered by those candidates that had had experience of observing Brownian motion.
notes.3b: Fewer candidates than expected were able to represent the random movement of a smoke particle and gain full credit. A common incorrect response was to draw a number of atoms representing a gas rather than on smoke particle.
notes.3c: A good number of candidates gained full credit for indicating collisions between air molecules and smoke particles.
notes.3d: There were many good answers from middle and higher ability candidates although in some misspelling prevented credit from being given.
notes.4a: A correct response was usually stated.
notes.4b: Many candidates scored three of the available marking points, identifying the use of planks or a ladder to increase surface area and reduce pressure. Few candidates made use of pressure = force per unit area or the idea of spreading the load. In a small number of cases, candidates gave an incorrect response by referring to the use of skates.
notes.5a: The correct answer was stated by the majority of better prepared candidates, however, there were significant numbers who gave the temperature displayed by the thermometer.
notes.5b: Candidates usually gained some credit for their responses but few gained full credit. Common misconceptions were that the ceiling was closer to the sun or ‘heat rises’ (rather than hot air). Very few responses included any mention of expansion.
notes.5c: The majority of candidates gained some credit for a partial response to this question. A significant number of candidates did not include any mention of the thread withdrawing towards the bulb.
notes.5d: A correct response was usually given.
notes.6ai: A significant number of candidates were unable to identify the angle of incidence and angle of reflection correctly.
notes.6aii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer to this question. Cambridge International General Certificate of Secondary Education 0625 Physics June 2014
notes.6aiii: The majority gave a correct response in terms of the periscope being used in a submarine. In some cases there were responses that were unclear or suggested that the periscope was for seeing things far away or above the observer.
notes.6bi: Very few candidates could be awarded credit for their response to this question. A common misconception was to identify the focal points rather than the focal lengths. A significant number indicated the distance between F and F without making clear that this was two focal lengths. 1 2
notes.6bii: Few candidates appreciated that the ray had to go through the focal point. A greater proportion of candidates were aware that there would be refraction, however some responses were poorly represented and could not be given credit.
notes.6biii: Only the better prepared candidates gained credit for their responses to this question.
notes.8ai: The correct answer was usually stated. A significant number of candidates, however, attempted to calculate a value for the current.
notes.8aii: A good proportion of the better prepared candidates gained full credit for their responses to this question. The most common errors were in rearranging the equation V= I R and the omission of the unit.
notes.8aiii: Very few candidates correctly indicated that the current would be 0.6 A. Common misconceptions included 1.2 A and 0.3 A.
notes.8bi: A good number of the able candidates gave correct responses to this question.
notes.8bii: Circuit diagrams were usually well drawn and included a component in series with the lamp. The better candidates obtained full credit for including the accepted symbol for a variable resistor, a rectangle with a strike-through arrow.
notes.10a: Many candidates gained credit for their response to this question. The most common incorrect responses were copper and steel.
notes.10b: This calculation was done well, indicating that candidates of differing abilities had all been well prepared for a question of this type. Many of those who did not give a correct response omitted to show their working and so were unable to gain any credit.
notes.11a: Many candidates scored full credit, although weaker candidates gave responses in terms of the structure of an atom, stating neutrons, protons and electrons.
notes.11b: A high proportion of candidates gained credit for at least two of the three marking points allocated to this question. A common misconception was the statement that gamma was the most easily absorbed radiation.
notes.11c: Only the very best candidates scored well on this question. Candidates seemed to be unclear about half life and how this would affect the numbers of particles remaining and decaying.
